hook.text: About 8% of men and 0.5% of women see a different color world. Red and green often merge into muddy brown.

buildup.text: Most color blindness is caused by a missing or altered cone type, inherited on the X chromosome.

discovery.text: John Dalton described his own color blindness in 1794. DNA from his preserved eyes confirmed he lacked green cones.

twist.text: Color-blind people often develop superior sensitivity to texture and brightness differences as compensation.

climax.text: In WWII, color-blind soldiers spotted camouflaged targets that normal-vision soldiers missed completely.

punchline.text: Seeing fewer colors can sometimes mean seeing more.

quiz.question: Why are men more often color blind?
options: The gene is on the X chromosome

details.summary: Color blindness, or color vision deficiency, affects about 8 percent of males and 0.5 percent of females. Most commonly, one type of cone cell does not function properly, making it difficult to distinguish red from green. Complete color blindness is extremely rare.
details.whyItMatters: Color blindness affects millions and has practical implications for design, safety signals, and career access. Designing for color accessibility benefits everyone.
takeaways: About 8 percent of males have some color vision deficiency
Red-green deficiency is the most common form by far
Design should never rely on color alone to convey information

faq.question: Do colorblind people see in black and white?
faq.answer: Almost never. Most colorblind people see colors but confuse certain pairs, typically red and green. They still see blues, yellows, and many other hues normally. Complete achromatopsia, seeing only gray, affects roughly 1 in 30,000 people and involves all cone types failing.

faq.question: Why is color blindness more common in males?
faq.answer: The genes for red and green cone pigments are on the X chromosome. Males have only one X, so a single defective gene causes color blindness. Females have two X chromosomes, so a working copy on one can compensate for a defective copy on the other.
